clinicalPearls: Caused by migrating plerocercoid (sparganum) larvae of Spirometra tapeworms, with humans as accidental intermediate hosts
Acquired by drinking water containing infected copepods, eating raw or undercooked frog, snake or other paratenic hosts, or applying raw amphibian flesh as a traditional poultice
The larva does not mature but migrates through tissues, producing a slowly moving, sometimes painful subcutaneous nodule that may appear and disappear
Ocular sparganosis causes periorbital swelling, pain and lid oedema, while cerebral sparganosis can cause seizures, headache and focal neurological deficits
Peripheral eosinophilia is common and imaging may show a migrating or serpiginous track or an enhancing granuloma
Definitive treatment is surgical removal of the whole larva; anthelmintic drugs are generally ineffective against the tissue-dwelling sparganum
Prevention includes drinking safe water, cooking meat thoroughly and avoiding the practice of applying raw amphibian tissue to wounds or eyes
reference.pathophysiology: Spirometra species are diphyllobothriid tapeworms whose adults live in cats, dogs and other carnivores. Their life cycle uses copepods as first intermediate hosts and amphibians, reptiles and other vertebrates as second intermediate or paratenic hosts harbouring the plerocercoid larva, the sparganum. Humans become accidental hosts by swallowing infected copepods in water, by eating raw or undercooked intermediate hosts, or by direct inoculation when raw frog or snake flesh is applied to skin, eyes or wounds as a poultice. The larva cannot mature in humans; instead it migrates through subcutaneous tissue, muscle, the eye or the central nervous system, provoking a local inflammatory and eosinophilic reaction with granuloma formation and, in the brain, surrounding oedema and mass effect. The living, motile larva accounts for the characteristic migratory and space-occupying features of the disease.
additionalDifferentials: Cutaneous larva migrans and other migratory helminth infection
Neurocysticercosis and other cerebral cystic or granulomatous disease
Coenurosis and hydatid disease of the central nervous system or soft tissue
Orbital cellulitis or other periorbital inflammatory lesion
additionalInvestigations: MRI or CT to localise migrating tracks, granulomas or intracranial lesions
Serology for sparganum antigens where available
Histological examination of the excised larva to confirm the diagnosis
Ophthalmological assessment in suspected ocular disease
Exclusion of other cystic cestode infection by appropriate serology
redFlags: Seizures or focal neurological signs indicating cerebral involvement
An enlarging or migrating intracranial lesion with mass effect
Recurrent or incompletely excised larva with persistent symptoms
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is good when a subcutaneous or ocular larva is completely removed, but cerebral sparganosis can cause lasting neurological deficits and may recur if the larva is not fully excised.
pitfalls: Relying on anthelmintic drugs, which rarely eradicate the tissue-dwelling sparganum
Incomplete surgical removal leaving viable larva and causing relapse
Mistaking a migrating subcutaneous nodule for a benign lipoma or cyst
Overlooking the history of raw-flesh poultice application or untreated water consumption
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Complete surgical excision of the entire larva is the definitive and curative treatment
Anthelmintic drugs are generally ineffective against the tissue-dwelling sparganum and are not relied upon
Corticosteroids to reduce peri-lesional inflammation and oedema, particularly in cerebral disease
Antiepileptic drugs to control seizures arising from cerebral sparganosis
Neurosurgical or ophthalmological referral for central nervous system or ocular larvae
Preventive advice: avoid drinking untreated water, eating raw or undercooked frog or snake, and applying raw amphibian poultices
Confirm complete removal and follow up, as incompletely excised larvae may recur
